title: Human Evolutionary History: An African Origin and Archaic Ancestry

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A dated volcanic ash layer lies above a fossil. What does the ash's date tell you about the fossil's age?
cards.back: Only a minimum age: the fossil is at least about that old.
cards.why: The ash settled after the bone was buried, so its eruption age bounds the fossil from below; it is not a direct date of the fossil.
cards.quote: An ash above a bone gives only a minimum age.

cards.front: Why do long inherited Neanderthal DNA segments in a human genome indicate recent mixing?
cards.back: Recombination breaks inherited Neanderthal DNA into shorter pieces every generation, so pieces stay long only when few generations have passed since the mixing.
cards.quote: recombination breaks inherited Neanderthal DNA into shorter pieces, so long pieces mean recent mixing.

cards.front: Genome X has much longer average Neanderthal segments than genome Y. A student concludes that X carries more Neanderthal ancestry than Y. Evaluate the conclusion.
cards.back: It does not follow. Segment length dates the mixing (X's was more recent), but it says nothing about how much ancestry came across, nor where or how often mixing happened.
cards.quote: longer segments do not mean more Neanderthal ancestry.

cards.front: In the multiregional model of human evolution, how did Homo sapiens arise?
cards.back: Populations in several regions evolved into Homo sapiens from older local groups while staying linked by gene flow.
cards.quote: populations in several regions evolved into Homo sapiens from older local groups while staying linked by gene flow.
cards.section: An African origin, without one birthplace or birthday

cards.front: What do genomes of living and ancient people show about where Homo sapiens arose, and how has the picture changed?
cards.back: They strongly support an African origin: living people trace most of their ancestry to African populations. The current picture is a braid of connected populations rather than one founding group.
cards.quote: Genomes of living and ancient people now strongly support the African origin instead: living people trace most of their ancestry to African populations.
cards.section: An African origin, without one birthplace or birthday

cards.front: In a large worldwide sample, individuals from {{c1::African-ancestry}} populations carried the greatest numbers of variant sites.
cards.quote: in a large worldwide sample, individuals from African-ancestry populations carried the greatest numbers of variant sites.
cards.section: An African origin, without one birthplace or birthday

cards.front: What is ancient DNA, and what comparison does it allow?
cards.back: Genetic sequence recovered from bones tens of thousands of years old; it lets you compare an extinct population with living people site by site.
cards.quote: Ancient DNA is genetic sequence recovered from bones tens of thousands of years old
cards.section: An African origin, without one birthplace or birthday

cards.front: Which Jebel Irhoud features look modern, which look primitive, and what does the mosaic show?
cards.back: Face, mandible and teeth align with anatomically modern humans; the neurocranium (braincase) and endocranial shape are more primitive. Modern anatomy did not arrive as one package.
cards.quote: while the neurocranium (the braincase) and endocranial shape are more primitive
cards.section: What the first film's dates leave out

cards.front: In the ABBA-BABA test using an African, a Eurasian, a Neanderthal and a chimpanzee, what role does the chimpanzee play, and what do A and B mean?
cards.back: The chimpanzee is the outgroup. Its allele at each site is called A (ancestral); the other allele is B (derived, a newer variant).
cards.quote: At each site, call the chimpanzee's allele A (ancestral) and the other B (derived, a newer variant).
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: In the quartet (African, Eurasian, Neanderthal, chimpanzee), which modern genome shares the derived allele with the Neanderthal at an ABBA site, and at a BABA site?
cards.back: ABBA: the Eurasian. BABA: the African. Only sites where the Neanderthal carries B are counted.
cards.quote: Look only at sites where the Neanderthal carries B, and ask which modern genome shares it.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: How can ABBA and BABA sites arise with no gene flow at all?
cards.back: Incomplete lineage sorting: a variant born in the population ancestral to all three can, by chance, survive in two lines and be lost in the third.
cards.quote: Both patterns disagree with the population tree, and both can arise with no gene flow at all, through incomplete lineage sorting.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: A derived variant arises in the population ancestral to Africans, Eurasians and Neanderthals. By chance it survives in the Eurasian and Neanderthal lines and is lost in the African line. No interbreeding occurs. What site pattern results?
cards.back: An ABBA site (African A, Eurasian B, Neanderthal B, chimpanzee A), produced by incomplete lineage sorting rather than gene flow.
cards.quote: a variant born in the population ancestral to all three can, by chance, survive in the African and Neanderthal lines
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Populations split with no later gene flow, and their common ancestor was one randomly mating population. Which count should be larger, ABBA or BABA?
cards.back: Neither; the counts should come out even apart from noise, so D is expected to be 0.
cards.why: Chance favours neither modern genome, so incomplete lineage sorting makes the two patterns equally likely.
cards.quote: Chance favours neither modern genome, so incomplete lineage sorting makes ABBA and BABA equally likely
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Give the formula for the D statistic and its possible range.
cards.back: D = (N_ABBA - N_BABA) / (N_ABBA + N_BABA). It has no units and runs from -1 to +1.
cards.quote: D has no units; it runs from -1 to +1.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Hypothetical counts at sites where the Neanderthal carries the derived allele: ABBA = 700, BABA = 500. A block jackknife gives a standard error for D of 0.04. Compute D and Z, and judge significance by the usual threshold of an absolute Z above 3.
cards.back: D = (700 - 500) / (700 + 500) = 200 / 1,200 = about 0.17. Z = 0.167 / 0.04 = about 4.2. Above 3, so the asymmetry is unlikely to be chance.
cards.why: Z is how many standard errors D sits from the no-gene-flow null of 0.
cards.quote: Z is how many standard errors D sits from zero.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Why is a block jackknife, rather than treating each site as independent, used to get the standard error of D?
cards.back: Neighbouring sites are inherited together, so sites are not independent. The jackknife drops one large genomic block at a time and recomputes D.
cards.quote: Neighbouring sites are inherited together, so sites are not independent.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: A study reports D = 0.20, highly significant, for (African, Eurasian, Neanderthal, chimpanzee). A reader concludes the Eurasian genome is 20% Neanderthal. What is wrong?
cards.back: D is not an ancestry percentage. It measures the asymmetry between ABBA and BABA counts; an ancestry fraction needs a separate estimator.
cards.quote: D = 0.20 does not mean 20% Neanderthal ancestry.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Besides interbreeding, what could make ABBA exceed BABA, and what can D not tell you at all?
cards.back: Old population structure: Eurasian ancestors drawn from part of a subdivided African population closer to the Neanderthal lineage. D also says nothing about when gene flow happened.
cards.why: Segment length tests both the structure alternative and the timing.
cards.quote: if the ancestors of Eurasians came from a part of an old, subdivided African population that was closer to the Neanderthal lineage
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: Hypothetical counts in (African, Eurasian, Neanderthal, chimpanzee): ABBA = 450, BABA = 550, standard error of D = 0.05. Compute D and Z and interpret them against the no-gene-flow null.
cards.back: D = (450 - 550) / 1,000 = -0.10. Z = -0.10 / 0.05 = -2. An absolute Z of 2 is below 3, so the data do not reject D = 0.
cards.why: The null predicts D = 0; a negative D would lean toward the African sharing more derived alleles, but this one is within chance.
cards.quote: The no-gene-flow model above predicts D = 0.
cards.section: Counting the clue: the D statistic

cards.front: After one pulse of mixing with no later gene flow, introgressed segments average about {{c1::1/t Morgans}} after t generations.
cards.back: About 100/t centimorgans.
cards.quote: after one pulse of mixing with no later gene flow, segments average about 1/t Morgans after t generations
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: What is a Morgan, and what is a centimorgan?
cards.back: A Morgan is the stretch of chromosome that averages one crossover per generation; a centimorgan (cM) is a hundredth of it.
cards.quote: A Morgan is the stretch of chromosome that averages one crossover per generation
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: Why is a centimorgan not a fixed number of DNA bases, and what does segment dating need as a result?
cards.back: Crossovers are commoner in some regions than others, so dating uses a recombination map.
cards.quote: Crossovers are commoner in some regions than others, so a centimorgan is no fixed number of bases
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: Under a one-pulse model, an ancient genome's Neanderthal segments average 0.25 cM. Using about 100/t cM and 29 years per generation, roughly how long before this person lived did the mixing occur?
cards.back: t = 100 / 0.25 = 400 generations; 400 x 29 = 11,600 years before the person lived.
cards.why: Rests on the 1/t Morgan decay rule, which assumes one pulse and no later gene flow.
cards.quote: so the average is about 100/t cM.
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: An ancient Homo sapiens genome carries Neanderthal segments averaging about 20 cM. Roughly how many generations back was the Neanderthal ancestor, and what kind of contact does that imply?
cards.back: t = 100 / 20 = 5 generations: a Neanderthal ancestor in the individual's own family tree, a recent contact like that seen at Bacho Kiro.
cards.quote: a recent Neanderthal ancestor in each individual's own family tree
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: Do the Bacho Kiro, Ust'-Ishim and present-day segment lengths record one pulse of mixing seen at three times?
cards.back: No. Bacho Kiro's long segments come from a separate, recent contact beside older, shorter pieces, and whether Ust'-Ishim's mixing is the one living people carry is not settled.
cards.quote: Bacho Kiro's long segments come from a separate, recent contact, beside older, shorter pieces
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: Suppose no interbreeding occurred, and Neanderthal-like segments in non-Africans came from a structured African population that split from the Neanderthal line hundreds of thousands of years ago. Would a 45,000-year-old genome carry clearly longer such segments than a present-day genome?
cards.back: Barely: only about a tenth to a fifth longer.
cards.why: Under structure the shared pieces are as old as the split, and 45,000 years is small against hundreds of thousands.
cards.quote: living 45,000 years earlier makes them only about a tenth to a fifth longer
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: The Ust'-Ishim genome (about 45,000 years old) has Neanderthal segments roughly two to four times longer than present-day ones on average. Which explanation for the D-statistic surplus does this favour, and why?
cards.back: Recent interbreeding. Old structure predicts segments only about a tenth to a fifth longer in a 45,000-year-old genome; two to four times longer fits gene flow 7,000-13,000 years before he lived.
cards.why: Rests on the decay rule: segment length shrinks with generations since mixing.
cards.quote: Reviews treat segments longer in dated ancient genomes than old structure predicts as the strongest sign of recent interbreeding
cards.section: Segment length as a clock

cards.front: How does sequence divergence from sequenced Neanderthal genomes distinguish recent gene flow from old population structure?
cards.back: A recently introgressed segment should be close to the sequenced Neanderthals; under old structure, shared segments should be as divergent as the deep split between the lineages implies.
cards.quote: A segment that entered from Neanderthals recently should be close to the sequenced Neanderthal genomes
cards.section: Telling gene flow from old structure: divergence and model fitting

cards.front: Who are the Denisovans, and in which sampled present-day people does their ancestry survive most clearly?
cards.back: A population known mostly from DNA, sharing a common origin with Neanderthals; most clearly in the sampled present-day Melanesians.
cards.quote: Denisovan ancestry survives in living people too, most clearly in the sampled present-day Melanesians
cards.section: Denisovans, and a child of two groups

cards.front: A fossil genome has roughly equal ancestry from two archaic groups. What pattern, at sites where the two groups' genomes differ, would mark a first-generation offspring rather than a member of a long-mixed population, and why?
cards.back: DNA fragments overlapping such sites carry one allele of each kind, consistently across the genome.
cards.why: Each chromosome pair has one chromosome from each parent, and no generations of recombination have cut the two lineages' DNA together.
cards.quote: A first-generation offspring has had no generations in which the two lineages' DNA could be cut together
cards.section: Denisovans, and a child of two groups

cards.front: Suppose a first-generation Neanderthal-Denisovan offspring had carried Denisovan-type mitochondrial DNA. Which parent would have been which?
cards.back: The mother would have been Denisovan and the father Neanderthal, because mitochondrial DNA comes from the mother.
cards.quote: Mitochondrial DNA comes from the mother, so the mother was Neanderthal and the father Denisovan
cards.section: Denisovans, and a child of two groups

cards.front: Does Denisova 11 show that modern humans interbred with archaic groups?
cards.back: No. It shows two archaic groups interbreeding; the evidence that modern humans interbred with them comes from Homo sapiens genomes.
cards.quote: Denisova 11 shows two archaic groups interbreeding; evidence that modern humans interbred with them comes from the Homo sapiens genomes above.
cards.section: Denisovans, and a child of two groups

cards.front: {{c1::Adaptive introgression}} is an allele that entered by interbreeding and then rose in frequency because carriers did better in that environment.
cards.quote: This is adaptive introgression: an allele that entered by interbreeding and then rose in frequency because carriers did better in that environment.
cards.section: What the inherited DNA did: adaptive introgression

cards.front: What is a haplotype?
cards.back: A combination of alleles carried together along one chromosome region, often inherited together.
cards.quote: a haplotype is a combination of alleles carried together along one chromosome region, often inherited together
cards.section: What the inherited DNA did: adaptive introgression

cards.front: What does EPAS1 encode, and what did its haplotype structure in Tibetans compared with Han Chinese suggest?
cards.back: A transcription factor involved in the response to low oxygen. The haplotype structure supported introgression from Denisovans or a Denisovan-related population, helping adaptation to high altitude.
cards.quote: At EPAS1, which encodes a transcription factor involved in the response to low oxygen
cards.section: What the inherited DNA did: adaptive introgression

cards.front: Hypothetical: an immune-gene haplotype closely matches the Neanderthal genome, is absent from sampled African genomes, and sits at the same modest frequency in every sampled Eurasian population whatever their environment. Is this adaptive introgression?
cards.back: Introgression is supported, but adaptation is not shown. The definition also requires a rise in frequency because carriers did better in a particular environment, as EPAS1 rose only at high altitude.
cards.why: Rests on the definition: entry by interbreeding plus selection-driven rise in frequency.
cards.quote: The authors concluded that admixture supplied variation that helped humans adapt to new environments
cards.section: What the inherited DNA did: adaptive introgression

cards.front: Genetic data from many loci can assign individuals to the populations they were sampled from. Give two observations showing that this does not make races discrete groups.
cards.back: Between-population variation is modest, and two people from different populations can be more alike than two from the same one. Most common variants are shared worldwide.
cards.why: Assignment reflects the groups and categories a study chose to sample.
cards.quote: two people from different populations can be more alike than two from the same one
cards.section: One species: why genetic clustering does not make races

cards.front: What alternative did Ragsdale and colleagues (2023) offer for patterns attributed to an unsampled archaic population in Africa?
cards.back: Weakly structured stem populations connected by gene flow over hundreds of thousands of years can explain them. Whether an archaic contribution happened remains open.
cards.quote: weakly structured stem populations connected by gene flow over hundreds of thousands of years can explain patterns
cards.section: What remains open

cards.front: A new genome comes from a Homo sapiens individual who lived in Europe around 45,000 years ago. Design an analysis to ask whether this person had a Neanderthal ancestor and roughly how many generations back, and state the limits of the conclusion.
cards.back: Find stretches matching sequenced Neanderthal genomes closely, comparing with present-day genomes; measure their lengths (about 100/t cM); very long segments mean a few generations back. Test first-generation status by one allele of each kind across the genome. Conclusions apply to that individual only.
cards.why: How many contacts there were, and where, needs many genomes.
cards.quote: Keep the conclusion to that individual: how many contacts there were, and where, needs many genomes.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Fu and colleagues' single-pulse fit to Ust'-Ishim gave 232-430 generations. At 29 years per generation, how long before he lived was the gene flow, and roughly how long ago in total, given he lived about 45,000 years ago?
cards.back: 232 x 29 = 6,728 and 430 x 29 = 12,470 years, which the lesson rounds to 7,000-13,000 years. Adding 45,000 gives roughly 52,000-58,000 years ago.
cards.quote: Adding the Ust'-Ishim man's age of about 45,000 years to the 7,000-13,000-year interval
cards.section: Timing the Neanderthal gene flow

cards.front: What does the simple 1/t segment-length rule ignore?
cards.back: Selection, later gene flow and errors in the recombination map.
cards.quote: The simple 1/t rule also ignores selection, later gene flow and errors in the recombination map.
cards.section: Timing the Neanderthal gene flow

cards.front: Why do sampled African genomes carry more Neanderthal-related signal than once recognized?
cards.back: Partly migration back into Africa and partly earlier gene flow from modern humans into Neanderthals.
cards.quote: explained partly by migration back into Africa and by earlier gene flow from modern humans into Neanderthals
cards.section: Archaic ancestry beyond the main line

cards.front: Hypothetical: a positive, significant D is found, but Neanderthal-like segments are no longer in a 45,000-year-old genome than in present-day genomes, and they are as divergent from sequenced Neanderthals as the deep lineage split implies. Which history do these data favour?
cards.back: Old population structure rather than recent interbreeding. D alone cannot tell them apart; segment length and divergence both match the structure prediction here.
cards.why: Recent gene flow predicts longer segments in dated ancient genomes and close similarity to sequenced Neanderthals.
cards.quote: Under old structure, shared segments should be as divergent from the Neanderthal as the deep split between the lineages implies.
cards.section: Telling gene flow from old structure: divergence and model fitting

cards.front: Does the discovery of archaic admixture in living people vindicate the multiregional model over an African origin?
cards.back: No. It shows some gene flow from other human groups did happen, but most living ancestry still traces to Africa.
cards.quote: The archaic admixture now known shows that some gene flow from other human groups did happen, though most living ancestry still traces to Africa.
cards.section: The multiregional model, fairly stated
